title: Split verbs: ophalen, meenemen, opstaan
intro: Many everyday verbs have two parts, like op + halen. Sometimes the front part jumps to the end of the sentence, and sometimes it stays. This lesson shows each case, with lines from a normal family day.

notes.title: 1. In a simple sentence, the front part goes to the end
body: A split verb has a small front part such as op, mee, aan, uit, af, in or terug. In a simple sentence the main part sits in second place and the front part goes to the very end.
The front part carries the stress: OPhalen, MEEnemen. That stress tells you a verb will split.

notes.title: 2. When the verb is at the end, the parts stay together
body: After wil, moet, kan or ga, the main verb goes to the end. Then the two parts stay together as one word.
The same happens in a side sentence after dat, omdat, als or wanneer.

examples.nl: Ik moet haar om drie uur [ophalen].
examples.en: I have to pick her up at three.

examples.nl: Ik denk dat de les om vier uur [afloopt].
examples.en: I think the lesson ends at four.

notes.title: 3. Telling someone what to do
body: For a command, start with the main part of the verb. The front part still goes to the end.

notes.title: 4. In the past, ge- goes in the middle
body: In the past form, ge- goes between the two parts. You write it as one word: opgehaald, aangedaan, meegenomen, uitgezet.

notes.title: 5. With te, it splits into three words
body: After om, vergeet niet, zin hebben or proberen, a verb gets te in front. With a split verb, te goes between the two parts, and you write three separate words: op te halen, mee te nemen.

examples.nl: Vergeet niet om je handdoek [mee te nemen].
examples.en: Don't forget to bring your towel.

examples.nl: Ik heb geen zin om [op te staan].
examples.en: I don't feel like getting up.

notes.title: 6. Verbs that never split
body: Verbs that start with be-, ver-, ont-, her- or ge- never split. They get no ge- in the past either: betalen, vertellen, beginnen, vertrekken.
You can hear it: the stress is not on the front part. beTAlen, verTELlen, beGINnen.

cards.rule: ophalen: op goes to the end.

cards.nl: Ze staat elke dag om zeven uur op.
cards.en: She gets up at seven every day.
alts: Elke dag staat ze om zeven uur op.
cards.rule: opstaan: op goes to the end.
meenemen: mee goes to the end.
meedoen: a question starts with doe, and mee goes to the end.

cards.nl: De trein komt om vijf uur aan.
cards.rule: aankomen: aan goes to the end.
terugbellen: terug goes to the end.
zich aankleden: me stays after the verb, aan goes to the end.
afwassen: af goes to the end.
nadenken: na goes to the end.

cards.nl: Ik moet haar om drie uur ophalen.
cards.en: I have to pick her up at three.
alts: Om drie uur moet ik haar ophalen.
cards.rule: After moet, ophalen stays in one piece at the end.

cards.en: Can you put your coat on?
cards.rule: After kun, aandoen stays in one piece at the end.
After wil, meedoen stays in one piece.

cards.nl: Ik denk dat de les om vier uur afloopt.
cards.en: I think the lesson ends at four.
cards.rule: After dat, the verb goes to the end in one piece: afloopt.
Command: ruim first, op last.
Command: doe first, aan last.
Command: zet first, uit last.
Command: kijk first, uit last.

cards.en: Go ahead and take your coat off.
cards.rule: Command: trek first, uit last.
Past: ge- in the middle, opgehaald.
Past: ge- in the middle, meegenomen.

cards.en: I got up early this morning.
cards.rule: Past: opgestaan, with ben.
Past: aangekleed, with ge- in the middle.

cards.en: Did you turn the TV off?
cards.rule: Past: ge- in the middle, uitgezet.

cards.nl: Vergeet niet om je handdoek mee te nemen.
cards.en: Don't forget to bring your towel.
cards.rule: With te: mee te nemen, three words.

cards.nl: Ik heb geen zin om op te staan.
cards.en: I don't feel like getting up.
cards.rule: With te: op te staan, three words.
betalen starts with be-, so it never splits.
vertrekken starts with ver-, so it never splits.
vertellen: no split, and no extra ge- in the past.
